name: PlanetScale
license: Proprietary (built on Vitess, Apache 2.0; the `pscale` CLI is Apache 2.0)
summary: Managed MySQL on Vitess and managed Postgres, with schema changes shipped through branches and deploy requests.
intro: PlanetScale runs databases for you on AWS and Google Cloud, in three flavours. Vitess databases speak the MySQL protocol: your app connects to VTGate proxies, which work out which MySQL 8 instances hold the rows and send the query there. Each MySQL instance is paired with a `vttablet` process. Tables can be split across many such shards by a sharding key that Vitess calls a vindex, while the app still sees one database. Postgres databases are plain Postgres run by PlanetScale’s own operator, with PgBouncer for connection pooling and extensions such as pgvector, PostGIS and TimescaleDB. Neki, in platform preview since September 2026, puts Postgres shards behind routers that speak the Postgres wire protocol. A highly available cluster is a primary and two replicas across three availability zones, on network-attached disks (Amazon EBS or Google Persistent Disk) that can grow automatically, or on Metal: local NVMe drives that you size up front.

Schema changes follow a code-review workflow. A branch is an isolated copy of the database. On Vitess you change the schema on a development branch, open a deploy request, and PlanetScale applies it online by building a ghost table with the new schema, keeping it in sync, then swapping it in; for 30 minutes you can revert without losing writes made in between. There has been no free plan since April 2024. Pricing is by resources: a monthly price per cluster size, prorated to the millisecond, plus storage, backups and egress. In AWS us-east-1 a single-node Postgres starts at $5 a month, a highly available Postgres cluster at $15, a Vitess cluster at $39 and Metal at $50. Enterprise customers can run it single-tenant or inside their own AWS or GCP account.
strengths: Horizontal sharding for MySQL from Vitess, the system YouTube built and Slack, GitHub and Square adopted, behind one connection string
Schema changes go through reviewed deploy requests, run online without locking tables, and can be undone for 30 minutes
Metal’s local NVMe drives give unlimited IOPS with storage included in the cluster price; Postgres on Metal starts at $50 a month
Plain resource pricing with a public price list, 12 AWS and 7 GCP regions, and an option to run in your own cloud account
limits: No free tier since the Hobby plan was retired on 8 April 2024, and new accounts are capped at `PS-160` and `M-320` sizes until they have paid a $100 invoice

Vitess isn’t all of MySQL: no stored procedures, triggers or events, no `LOCK TABLES` or `LOAD DATA INFILE`, InnoDB only, every table needs a unique key, and no binlog replication to outside databases
Postgres branching lags Vitess: new branches start empty or from a backup, there are no deploy requests, and schema changes are copied to production by hand
Metal storage doesn’t grow on its own: the database turns read-only when 6 GB is left, and on GCP Metal starts at $559 a month
Network-attached storage is billed per instance, so a highly available Vitess cluster pays $1.50 per GB a month beyond the 10 GB included

snippet.title: Ship a schema change through a branch and a deploy request
source: # a Vitess (MySQL-compatible) database in Frankfurt; deploy requests need safe migrations
pscale database create shop --engine mysql --region eu-central --cluster-size PS_10 --wait
pscale branch safe-migrations enable shop main
# change the schema on an isolated development branch, not on production
pscale branch create shop add-order-notes --from main --wait
#   mysql> ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes VARCHAR(500) NULL;
# open a deploy request, review the diff, then apply it online
pscale deploy-request create shop add-order-notes --into main --notes 'Add order notes'
# changed your mind? revert within 30 minutes without losing new writes

story: In 2010 YouTube’s MySQL primary was running out of room. Read replicas bought time, then writes outgrew one server, so the app itself learned which shard held each row. Vitess moved that routing out of the application into a proxy that sits between the app and MySQL. It has been part of YouTube’s database infrastructure since 2011, grew to tens of thousands of MySQL nodes, and was adopted by Slack, Square and GitHub. It joined the CNCF in 2018 and graduated in November 2019.

Vitess’s co-creators and maintainers founded PlanetScale in 2018. The cloud product launched in beta in May 2021 as “the database for developers”, promising schema changes as easy as deploying code, and became generally available that November with a $50 million Series C.

In March 2024 CEO Sam Lambert chose profitability: the company laid off staff, mainly in sales and marketing, and retired the free Hobby plan. Since then PlanetScale has moved down the stack and across engines, with local NVMe Metal clusters in 2025, managed Postgres the same year, and Neki, sharded Postgres built from scratch rather than forked from Vitess, in 2026.

choices.choice: Build on Vitess instead of a new engine
choices.why: The founders had already scaled MySQL at YouTube with Vitess, and sharding behind a proxy keeps real MySQL underneath while the app sees one database.

choices.choice: Branches and deploy requests for schema changes
choices.why: Developers wanted a SQL database without being held back by managing its schema. Treating a schema change like code (a branch, a reviewed diff, a deploy, an undo) aims to make it feel as easy as deploying code.

choices.choice: Online migrations through a ghost table
choices.why: Copying data into a new table in the background and swapping it in avoids locking the live table, and keeping the old table in sync for 30 minutes makes a revert possible.

choices.choice: Local NVMe drives instead of network storage
choices.why: Every read and write on a network-attached volume crosses the network, and high IOPS cost extra. Local drives give lower latency and unlimited IOPS, at the price of choosing a drive size up front.

timeline.text: YouTube creates Vitess to scale its MySQL databases
Vitess co-creators found PlanetScale; Vitess joins the CNCF
PlanetScale’s cloud database enters beta in May, generally available in November
Layoffs and the end of the free Hobby plan (8 April)
Metal (local NVMe) in March; PlanetScale for Postgres in September
Neki, sharded Postgres, enters platform preview
